content.text:
No, performance isn't at the forefront today, and nothing in the repo would catch a regression. There are no benchmarks, no benchmark or timing tooling in the manifests, `justfile` or workflows, and no performance target in the docs.

**What the audit measured:** `callisto status` on a synthetic repo with 200 packages and 200 tags took 14.6 s (10 s of it system time). It spawned 604 git processes: 200 `rev-parse`, 200 `show`, 200 `log`, 1 `tag --list`. The cost grows roughly linearly with package count, so 500 packages would take over 30 s. A fast Rust CLI should do this in well under a second. Everything else below is estimated from the code, not measured.

**Where the time goes:**
- **Git process fan-out.** Most commands spawn git once or twice per package. The code answers per-package questions with per-package processes. A single `for-each-ref` for tags and one `git log --name-only` from the oldest tag would replace hundreds of spawns.
- **Every subprocess pays a 50 ms floor.** `runner.rs:518` sleeps 50 ms after the first poll, so a 3 ms `git rev-parse` costs 50 ms. The release path does this on every trust check.
- **The executor does serial work that could overlap.** Its read-only registry, tag and forge checks run one at a time, and it re-verifies git trust (about 7 spawns) before every operation, even ones that only observe. The audit estimates 25–40 minutes for a no-op rerun at 500 packages. I confirmed the trust re-check is in the loop but did not measure the total.
- **`release-pr decide` runs the full `status()` to read one boolean,** on every push to the base branch.
- **The A2 guard walks a manifest's whole history** before truncating it. PR #326 already replaced that with a path-limited walk.

**Why it hasn't shown up:** the test fixtures have 1–10 packages, and our own repo is small. At that size none of this matters. A monorepo with hundreds of packages would feel it in every CI run.

**What I'd do, in order:**
1. **Add a benchmark first.** A generated 200- and 1000-package repo, timed for `status`, `version --dry-run` and `release --dry-run`, run in CI with a threshold. Without it, any fix is unmeasured and the gains erode.
2. **Cheap high-return fixes:** `decide` reads the boolean, a 1–50 ms backoff instead of the 50 ms floor, one tag-to-commit map from `for-each-ref`, and one `git log --name-only` for change detection.
3. **Structural fixes:** a bounded thread pool for read-only preflight, and the trust re-check moved to just before an effect. The trust move changes when the stale-worktree guard fires, so that one needs your sign-off.

Step 1 plus the cheap fixes should take `status` at 200 packages from 14.6 s to around a second or less. Want me to start with the benchmark and those fixes as the next PR?
Can we use git in a way that amortizes the cost? Is that a background mode?? something thatdoesn't pay the cost for each?

Yes, but a background mode isn't the right tool. Amortizing within a single run gets nearly all of the gain.

**Why not a daemon:**
- CI starts cold every run, so a warm process saves nothing there.
- It adds stale-state risk, and ADR 3 deliberately keeps rerun logic free of persisted state.
- Git already has the useful long-lived pieces for local use: `core.fsmonitor` for fast `status`, and `git maintenance` for the commit-graph.

**What does work, all inside one command run:**
1. **One long-lived `git cat-file --batch` process.** It is a request/response pipe, so every blob lookup (a manifest at a tag, a manifest at a commit) costs a write and a read instead of a process spawn. The release code already has a private reader like this in `release_decision.rs`. Today's 400 `rev-parse` + `show` spawns for the tag index become 2 per package over one pipe.
2. **One bulk ref query.** `git for-each-ref refs/tags --format='%(refname:strip=2) %(*objectname) %(objectname)'` gives every tag and its peeled commit in a single call. That replaces the per-package `rev-parse` and the tag listing.
3. **One history pass.** A single `git log --name-only` from the oldest relevant tag, bucketed by package path, replaces one `git log` per package. This is the biggest win for `status`.
4. **Commit-graph with changed-path Bloom filters** (`git commit-graph write --reachable --changed-paths`) makes path-limited logs much faster on large histories. We can't count on it in a fresh CI clone, so I'd document it for local use and not depend on it.

Together these take the measured 604 spawns to roughly 5. The 14.6 s `status` run should land near a second.

**The shape to build:** a `GitSession` in `callisto_model::vcs`, created once per command. It holds the batch process, the ref snapshot and the history index. This also closes the architecture audit's finding that git access is forked outside `GitAccess`. Every caller then goes through one amortizing layer.

**Constraints:**
- ADR 5 says system git only, so no `gix` or `libgit2`. That rules out the in-process route and is consistent with this plan.
- Reusing a batch process needs care on Windows (unsupported anyway) and on crash handling. It should restart on EOF and fall back to one-shot calls.

I'd do the benchmark first, then `GitSession` with steps 1 to 3. Want me to start on that?

# 5. System git only

Status: Accepted (implemented in #145)

## Context

- Callisto reads commits, tags and staged changes, and creates and pushes tags.
- From 2026-08-03 `callisto-vcs` had two backends behind `GitDataSource`: native gix (`GitRepository`) and a shell fallback (`ShellGit`), with reads retrying through the shell on any native error (commit bb2a69cc4).
- The CLI already required a `git` binary: trust observation, staged changes and every fallback went through it (#145).

## Decision

Every Git command in the `callisto` binary runs the user's `git` through `CommandRunner`. `callisto_model::vcs` has one Git access type, `GitAccess`, and defines no backend trait; `GitAccess` implements callisto-model's `CommitWalker` for severity inference (`crates/callisto-vcs/src/lib.rs`). Git operations use the user's git config and identity, except release tags: with no identity set, the target commit's committer becomes the tagger, and `TagSignPolicy::ForceUnsigned` adds `--no-sign` (`crates/callisto-vcs/src/access.rs`). Workspace-root discovery looks for a `.git` entry on disk (`crates/callisto-graph/src/locate/root.rs`).

## Options considered

- **gix as the primary backend with a shell fallback (two backends)** — rejected in #145: "Two backends meant two semantics to keep in step (gix ignored TagSignPolicy) and 106 extra crates." The changeset adds: "every Git read and write already had to work through the `git` binary the CLI requires."
- **gix only** — not considered in #145. Reason not recorded.

## Consequences

- History walks use `git log --no-merges --full-history`, matching the gix commit sets; plain `git log` history simplification drops commits whose change a later merge discarded.
- Callisto depends on the installed git version and parses its output.
- Annotated tags work on runners with no git identity: the tagger falls back to the target commit's committer (#145).
- The managed release-PR action is outside this decision: it writes its commit and branch refs through the GitHub API (`.github/actions/callisto-action/scripts/create-or-update-release-pr.sh`).
- Today `release-pr commit-plan` reads staged bytes from the worktree, not the index (docs/projects/ROAD-TO-V1.md, v1 fix plan §1).

## Enforcement

- `callisto_model::vcs` has no gix dependency and one `GitAccess` type (`crates/callisto-model/src/vcs/access.rs`).
- Nothing bans gix in `deny.toml`; reintroducing it needs a new ADR.

## Revisit when

- A required Git operation is impossible or unacceptably slow through the binary, measured against the #145 numbers.
- Callisto must run where no `git` binary exists.

## Sources

- PR #145 (7ad333311): commit body, PR body, `.changeset/calm-foxes-pounce.md`
- Commit bb2a69cc4 (two-backend `GitDataSource` introduced)
- docs/00-design.md §15 `callisto-vcs` entry, describing the pre-#145 two-backend design (`git show 7ad333311^:docs/00-design.md`)

Track 0 spike completed 2026-08-05. Verdict: NO-GO.

**Why:** WASI returns ENOSYS for mmap(). Both `gix-odb` (loose objects) and `gix-pack` (packed objects) use memory-mapped I/O internally with no opt-in read-based fallback. Any gix object read from inside a WASM guest panics with `Find(PackedOpen(Io(Kind(Unsupported))))`.

**What works in WASI:** `gix-ref` (HEAD resolution, branch/tag ref reads) uses regular file I/O and works fine.

**Blocker will not self-resolve** without WASI gaining mmap support or gix-odb gaining an opt-in read-fallback — neither is imminent.

**Consequence for Track C exec-seam:** callisto-moon must use `warpgate_pdk::exec_command` (moon's sanctioned host-exec bridge) for any operation requiring git object reads (commit messages, tree diffs, etc.). A hybrid using native gix-ref for lightweight ref lookups + host exec for commit data is technically possible but adds complexity for minimal gain — the simpler path is host-exec for all git operations.

**Evidence:** Prior spike at `ffc922d`, probe at `/tmp/gix-wasm-probe/`, documented in `crates/callisto-moon/examples/gix_wasm_spike.rs`.

**How to apply:** When implementing Track C exec-seam, use `warpgate_pdk::exec_command` exclusively. Do not re-attempt native gix object reads without new upstream information (WASI mmap support or gix-odb read-fallback).

It wasn't auth, and it wasn't performance. Both ADRs record the reasons.

**Why gix went away (ADR 5, PR #145):**
- **Two backends meant two sets of behavior to keep in step.** gix ignored `TagSignPolicy`, so tag creation behaved differently depending on which backend ran.
- **gix added 106 crates.**
- **The CLI needed the `git` binary anyway** for trust observation, staged changes and every fallback.
- The ADR doesn't record why "gix only" wasn't considered.
- **No performance numbers were recorded in the ADR.** I couldn't find any #145 numbers, so I can't say what was measured then.

**Why WASM went away (ADR 6, PR #142):** the Track 0 spike found gix object reads panic inside WASI, because `gix-odb` and `gix-pack` use mmap and WASI returns ENOSYS. That was one of several reasons to drop the moon WASM extension, which also forced a second command surface, a second release artifact and wasmtime into the dependency tree. Callisto now ships one native binary, so the WASI blocker no longer constrains anything.

**What this means for performance:** the speed question can be reopened, and ADR 5 anticipates it. Its revisit trigger is "a required Git operation is unacceptably slow through the binary". A 14.6 s `status` at 200 packages looks like that, though I haven't re-measured against whatever #145 measured.

I can't say gix is "way faster" for us without measuring it. It avoids process spawns and can use the commit-graph in-process, so it likely wins on reads. A batched system-git layer may close most of that gap with no new dependency.

**Suggested order:**
1. Build the benchmark, then `GitSession` (batch pipe, bulk refs, single history pass). That needs no new ADR.
2. If the result is still short of the target, measure gix for reads only, behind the same `GitAccess` API. Writes, tagging, signing and auth stay on system git, which avoids the two-semantics problem. That path needs a new ADR the owner accepts, as AGENTS.md requires for reversing an ADR.

If you'd rather go to gix reads now, I can write the benchmark so it runs both paths on the same fixtures and the numbers settle it.

input.content:
Callisto has no way to see how its commands scale with workspace size, and an audit found they spawn git once or twice per package. This adds the measurement so the fixes that follow have numbers.

- `just bench` generates a tagged Cargo workspace of N packages with 2N later commits and a changeset on every tenth package, then times `status`, `version --dry-run` and `release --dry-run` against the release binary. It reports the median of three runs and the number of git processes each started, counted from git's own trace. `CALLISTO_BENCH_PACKAGES=50,200` picks the sizes and `CALLISTO_BENCH_SHAPES=1` lists which git commands the processes were.
- The workspace is built by `callisto_fixtures::perf::ScaledWorkspace` with one `git fast-import`, so 500 packages with annotated tags take under a second to set up.
- `AGENTS.md` points to it: a change that adds a git process per package should fail review.

Baseline on this branch, release build, 200 packages:

| command | median ms | git processes |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `status` | 2001 | 405 |
| `version --dry-run` | 5692 | 1010 |
| `release --dry-run` | 3244 | 604 |

The process count grows linearly: about 2, 5 and 3 per package. At 100 packages the processes are almost all three patterns: a manifest read at every tag when the tag index is built (`rev-parse --verify` plus `show`), a second tag resolution per package during release planning, and a `diff --cached --quiet` per file in `version`. The next PR removes them.

This does not add a regression gate yet. The gate belongs with the fixes, once there are budgets worth enforcing.

`status`, `version` and `release --dry-run` started two to five git processes per package. This reads the same data in a constant number of calls. Stacked on #327, which adds the benchmark these numbers come from.

Release build, median of three, generated workspace with a tag per package and two commits per package:

| packages | command | before ms | after ms | git processes before | after |
| ---: | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 200 | `status` | 2001 | 78 | 405 | 6 |
| 200 | `version --dry-run` | 5692 | 102 | 1010 | 10 |
| 200 | `release --dry-run` | 3244 | 82 | 604 | 6 |
| 500 | `status` | not run | 168 | not run | 6 |
| 500 | `version --dry-run` | not run | 184 | not run | 10 |
| 500 | `release --dry-run` | not run | 170 | not run | 6 |

What changed:

- The tag index read the manifest at every package's newest tag with a `rev-parse` and a `show` each. It now reads them all with one `git cat-file --batch`. The batch parser, with its fail-closed framing checks, moved out of `release_decision.rs` into `commands/git_batch.rs` and is shared by both callers.
- Release planning and commit inference resolved each package's tag with its own `rev-parse`. The tag index now reads every tag's commit with one `git for-each-ref` the first time it is asked.
- `version` checked every manifest's staged state with its own `git diff --cached --quiet` and read each manifest at HEAD with two processes. It now reuses the index diff it already ran and reads the manifests in one batch.
- `tests/git_process_count_tests.rs` fails when `status`, `version --dry-run` or `release --dry-run` start a different number of git processes for 6 packages than for 30. A change that adds a process per package now fails CI.

A failed batch read is not an error: the lookups fall back to one read at a time, as before. Not changed: the history walk for a package whose manifest is missing at its tag still searches the tree three times per package, and the executor's per-operation git work. Both are next.

The bulk-reads work cut git processes to a constant, and full CI is running now.

| at 200 packages | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `status` | 2001 ms, 405 git processes | 78 ms, 6 |
| `version --dry-run` | 5692 ms, 1010 | 102 ms, 10 |
| `release --dry-run` | 3244 ms, 604 | 82 ms, 6 |

At 500 packages all three run in 168–184 ms, still with 6–10 processes. I'll commit and open the PR, stacked on the benchmark PR #327, once `just ci` reports `exit=0`.
Feels like we could use gix or something else if there is a better library for anything that is not auth related?

Probably not worth it for the work we've batched. I'll measure how much time is still in git before saying so for certain.

**What the batching changed.** The earlier case for gix was that every package paid a process spawn. We now spawn 6–10 git processes per command regardless of workspace size. At 200 packages the whole command takes about 80 ms, and I estimate 5 ms per spawn, so spawns are roughly 30–50 ms of that. The rest is Callisto's own parsing and graph work, which gix wouldn't touch.

**What gix would still save:**
- The fixed spawn cost, maybe 30–50 ms per command.
- A possible edge on very deep history walks. That is unmeasured, and git's C implementation is already fast at `log`.

**What it would cost (from ADR 5):**
- 106 extra crates.
- Two sets of semantics to keep in step. gix has already diverged from git once on tag signing.
- The `--full-history` commit-set behavior would have to match exactly.
- Reversing an ADR needs a new ADR you accept.

**Auth isn't the dividing line.** gix handles reads well and writes, tagging and signing worse. Reads-only gix is possible behind `GitAccess`, but it only pays if git time is still a large share of what's left.

**What I'll do.** I'll add a "time in git" column to the benchmark, summed from git's own trace timestamps, so we can see what share of the 80–180 ms is git versus Callisto. If git is under about 30% of the remaining time, the next gains are in our own parsing and allocation, not the git layer. If it's much larger, the gix read experiment is worth running behind `GitAccess` with this benchmark as the judge. The full CI for the bulk-reads PR is still running, so I'll make that change once it finishes, to avoid disturbing its build.

I'm assuming you mean the git layer: what if it were in-process or cached instead of shelling out. Everything below is an estimate until I add the "time in git" measurement, which waits for the running CI to finish.

| approach | what it removes | rough result at 200–500 packages |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Today, batched system git | the per-package processes | 80–180 ms, 6–10 processes |
| gix for reads | the fixed spawn cost, about 30–50 ms per command | roughly 40–140 ms. That is a modest gain, because the rest is Callisto's own work |
| Cache parsed results by git object id | re-reading and re-parsing unchanged manifests on a warm run | helps local runs. CI starts cold, so it gains nothing there |
| Do less work per command | reading tags and manifests the command doesn't need | depends on the command, and needs a profile to size |

- **Why gix helps less than it sounds:** `status` at 200 packages is 78 ms with 6 git processes. Even if git were free, I'd expect 40–50 ms of Callisto's own time to remain: walking the filesystem, parsing 200+ manifests, building the graph and running the cascade.
- **The cache is safe in principle.** Git objects are immutable, so a cache keyed by object id can't go stale. ADR 3 only forbids persisted *release execution* state, not a read cache. It would need its own ADR, and it only pays off on warm local runs.

**What I'll do once CI finishes:** add the git-time column to the benchmark, and take a CPU profile of `status` at 500 packages to see the actual split between git, filesystem walk, parsing, and graph work. If git is a large share of the 168 ms, the gix read experiment is justified, with the benchmark as the judge. If parsing and walking dominate, the next gains are in our own allocation and parsing, and gix wouldn't help. Tell me if you meant a different part, such as the executor or the registry reads.
What of other libraries? Are there better choices?

content.text:
For the most part the libraries are already the fast, standard choices. The wins are in how we use them and in two additions. Before I could say what's worth changing, I had to check what we use today.

**Already the right tool:**
- **`ignore`** is the walker ripgrep uses, and the best-in-class option. We use the sequential `WalkBuilder` (no `build_parallel` anywhere), so there is headroom without changing library.
- **`toml_edit`** is required for format-preserving writes (invariant 2), and nothing faster does that. `serde_json` with `preserve_order` is needed for key order. `globset` and `semver` are the standard picks. `sha2` is fixed by the wire digests.
- **`petgraph`** is still a dependency in the `callisto-graph` manifest, but only `toposort.rs` uses it (`tarjan_scc`). The stacked PRs #319/#320 move that onto `michi-graph`. Once they merge, it can go.

**Changes worth testing, in order of expected return:**
1. **A faster allocator on the musl build.** We ship `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`, and musl's default malloc is very slow for allocation-heavy code like parsing hundreds of manifests. `mimalloc` there is a few lines and often a double-digit speedup. I can't measure it on this Mac, so it needs a Linux CI run of the benchmark.
2. **Parse manifests in parallel.** `rayon` over the discovered manifests could cut the parse phase 2–4× on a multi-core machine. At 500 packages the phase is probably a double-digit share of 168 ms, but that needs the profile.
3. **Parallel directory walk** via `ignore`'s existing parallel walker. This only matters on very large trees, since the walk is I/O-bound and our fixture is small.
4. **Check for double parsing.** Both `toml` and `toml_edit` are dependencies. `toml` is used for config, the matrix and the registry argv. If any file is parsed by both, that is waste I can remove without a new library.

I don't know yet which of these matters, because I haven't profiled where the remaining 80–180 ms goes. That profile is the next step once CI finishes: it decides between the allocator, parallel parsing, or nothing, and it is also the evidence for or against gix. I won't add a dependency on a guess.

content.text:
Full CI is running for the single-pass history change. While it runs, here is where performance stands, because the benchmark overturned my earlier numbers:

- **My earlier "6 git processes" result was an artifact.** The fixture tagged every package on one commit. In a realistic repo with independent versioning, `status` at 500 packages took **11.7 s**, with 500 separate `git log` processes (9.7 s of it).
- **With the single pass it's 206 ms.** That is 505 git processes down to 10 and about 57× faster. A unit test compares it against the old per-tag walk across a merge and a side-branch tag, and the answers match.
- **Git time still matters at scale.** At 2000 packages `status` is about 1.2 s, with 646 ms in git: one `git log` over 4000 commits (274 ms) and the manifest batch (138 ms). The batch asks by tag name, which makes git try several ref spellings per name. Asking by commit hash, as the `version` batch does, is about five times cheaper per object.

Next, once this ships: the commit-hash batch plus a single tag listing (it replaces `tag --list` and `for-each-ref`, and the test fakes need updating), then a CPU profile of the roughly half of the time that isn't git.

import subprocess, sys, shutil, os

packages = int(sys.argv[1])
extra = int(sys.argv[2])
root = sys.argv[3]
TS = 1_700_000_000

shutil.rmtree(root, ignore_errors=True)
os.makedirs(root)

def git(*args):
    subprocess.run(["git", *args], cwd=root, check=True)

git("init", "-q", "-b", "main")
out = bytearray()

def data(text):
    b = text.encode()
    return b"data %d\n" % len(b) + b + b"\n"

def commit(mark, message, files):
    out.extend(f"commit refs/heads/main\nmark :{mark}\ncommitter Bench <bench@example.com> {TS + mark} +0000\n".encode())
    out.extend(data(message))
    for path, content in files:
        out.extend(f"M 100644 inline {path}\n".encode())
        out.extend(data(content))

def manifest(i):
    text = f'[package]\nname = "pkg-{i}"\nversion = "1.0.0"\nedition = "2021"\n'
    if i % 4 != 0:
        text += f'\n[dependencies]\npkg-{i-1} = {{ path = "../pkg-{i-1}", version = "1.0.0" }}\n'
    return text

files = [("Cargo.toml", '[workspace]\nmembers = ["crates/*"]\nresolver = "2"\n'), ("callisto.toml", "# bench\n")]
for i in range(packages):
    files.append((f"crates/pkg-{i}/Cargo.toml", manifest(i)))
    files.append((f"crates/pkg-{i}/src/lib.rs", "pub fn f() {}\n"))
mark = 1
commit(mark, "chore: scaffold the workspace", files)
for step in range(extra):
    mark += 1
    target = (step * 7919) % packages
    commit(mark, f"fix: edit pkg-{target}", [(f"crates/pkg-{target}/src/lib.rs", f"pub fn f() {{}}\n// edit {step}\n")])
for i in range(packages):
    name = f"pkg-{i}@1.0.0"
    message = f"Release {name}\n"
    target = 1 + i % (extra + 1)
    out.extend(f"tag {name}\nfrom :{target}\ntagger Bench <bench@example.com> {TS} +0000\n".encode())
    out.extend(data(message))
mark += 1
commit(mark, "chore: add changesets", [(f".changeset/bench-{i}.md", f'---\n"cargo/pkg-{i}": patch\n---\n\nFix pkg-{i}.\n') for i in range(0, packages, 10)])

subprocess.run(["git", "fast-import", "--quiet"], cwd=root, input=bytes(out), check=True)
git("reset", "-q", "--hard", "main")
git("remote", "add", "origin", "https://github.com/example/bench.git")

input.content:
`status` and `version` started one `git log` for every distinct tag commit. With independent versioning, where each package is released at its own time, that is one process per package. This reads the history once. Stacked on #328.

The benchmark fixture was hiding this: it tagged every package on a single commit. It now spreads the tags over history, as independent releases do. On that fixture, release build, 500 packages:

| command | before ms | after ms | git processes before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `status` | 11717 | 206 | 505 | 10 |

At 2000 packages `status` takes about 1.2 s, of which 646 ms is git: one `git log` over 4000 commits and the manifest batch. That is the next target. There is no "before" for 2000, because the old code was already in the minutes.

How it works:

- `GitAccess::change_history` finds a common ancestor of all the tag commits with `git merge-base --octopus`, then reads the commits after it with one `git log --name-only --cc`, which also gives each commit's parents. `ChangeHistory::paths_since(tag)` walks parents in memory to drop the tag's ancestors and returns what the rest changed.
- `changed_since_last_tag` uses it, plus one `git diff --name-only HEAD` for uncommitted changes. The tag commits come from the tag index's single `git for-each-ref`.
- A merge counts for the paths where it differs from every parent, as `--cc` reports them. The old code reached those only through its worktree diff.
- If a tag does not resolve to a commit, or git cannot produce the history in bulk, the old walk per tag commit runs instead. A test builds a history with a merge and a tag on a side branch and checks both give the same answer.

`tests/git_process_count_tests.rs` now catches this: the fixture spreads tags, so a `git log` per tag commit makes 6 packages and 30 packages start different numbers of processes. The benchmark also reports time spent in git and, with `CALLISTO_BENCH_SHAPES=1`, the time per command.

import subprocess, time, os

repo = "/Users/gabe/.claude/jobs/15c732d1/tmp/profile-repo"
n = 4000

def run(args, inp=None):
    return subprocess.run(args, cwd=repo, input=inp, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout

# tag -> peeled commit, like for-each-ref gives us
rows = run(["git", "for-each-ref", "--format=%(refname:strip=2) %(*objectname)", "refs/tags"]).splitlines()
commit = dict(line.split(" ", 1) for line in rows)

def specs(kind):
    out = []
    for i in range(n):
        tag = f"pkg-{i}@1.0.0"
        path = f"crates/pkg-{i}/Cargo.toml"
        if kind == "name":
            out.append(f"{tag}:./{path}")
        elif kind == "fullref":
            out.append(f"refs/tags/{tag}:./{path}")
        else:
            out.append(f"{commit[tag]}:./{path}")
    return "\n".join(out) + "\n"

for kind in ["name", "fullref", "sha"]:
    data = specs(kind)
    best = 1e9
    for _ in range(3):
        t = time.time()
        run(["git", "cat-file", "--batch"], data)
        best = min(best, time.time() - t)
    print(f"{kind:8s} {best*1000:7.0f} ms for {n} objects")

Here is what the profile shows, with the caveats:

**At 4000 packages and 8000 commits, `status` is about 2.2 s, and 74% of it is waiting on git.** My first profile was misleading: it missed the start of the run and showed a git-dominated picture that was incomplete. The corrected one found two problems in code I had just written, and I've fixed both:
- The aggregation was quadratic (about 640 ms): it cloned paths per tag and tested every path against every package. It's now linear, with each package getting a list of the commits that touched it.
- A tag on an unmerged branch was treated as "everything after it". The old code counted a package as changed when its files differ from the tag, which includes a hotfix that `HEAD` lacks. The rule is now exact: a commit counts if it is reachable from `HEAD` or the tag, but not both. Tests cover a merge and a hotfix branch, each checked against the old per-tag walk.

I also fixed the tag-glob matching (a sorted index replaces testing every glob against every tag, worth about 220 ms), and I retracted my earlier claim that commit hashes would make the manifest batch 5× faster: measured, it's about 25%, so I dropped it.

**What's left** is git doing real work (`git log` over 8000 commits, 730 ms) and the sequential directory walk (230 ms). The timings are noisy, because another process on this machine is compiling. I'll push the redesign onto PR #330 once CI reports `exit=0`.

input.content:
`status` and `version` started one `git log` for every distinct tag commit. With independent versioning, where each package is released at its own time, that is one process per package. This reads the history once, and answers per tag in memory. Stacked on #328.

The benchmark fixture was hiding this: it tagged every package on a single commit. It now spreads the tags over history, as independent releases do. On that fixture, release build, 500 packages:

| command | before ms | after ms | git processes before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `status` | 11717 | 206 | 505 | 10 |

At 4000 packages and 8000 commits `status` takes about 2.2 s. A CPU sample of that run puts 74% of it in waiting on git: the one `git log` over 8000 commits (about 730 ms), `merge-base` and `diff` (180 ms), the manifest batch (255 ms) and the tag list (65 ms). The rest is the directory walk (230 ms, mostly `opendir` and `open`). The old code was already in the minutes there, so there is no meaningful "before".

How it works:

- `GitAccess::change_history` finds a common ancestor of all the tag commits with `git merge-base --octopus`, then reads `HEAD` and every tag commit back to it with one `git log --topo-order --name-only --cc`, which also gives each commit's parents. Many tags go through stdin so the argument list stays short.
- `ChangeHistory::any_differing(tag, commits)` says whether any of a package's touching commits separates `HEAD` from the tag: reachable from one and not the other. For a tag on a line of history that is "after the tag". For a tag on a branch that was never merged it also counts the branch's own commits, because `HEAD` then lacks them. That matches the old rule that a package whose files differ from its tag has changed. A line of history with no merges needs no graph walk.
- `changed_since_last_tag` builds, per package, the list of commits that touched it with one lookup per path ancestor, instead of testing every path against every package. It also reads uncommitted changes with one `git diff --name-only HEAD`.
- If a tag does not resolve to a commit, or git cannot produce the history in bulk, the old walk per tag commit runs instead. Tests build a history with a merge and tags on a side branch, and one with a hotfix branch that was never merged, and check both give the same answer as that walk.
- The tag index tests a template's glob only against the run of tags that begin with its literal prefix, found by binary search in a sorted list, instead of against every tag. At 4000 packages that was about 220 ms of CPU.

A merge counts for the paths where it differs from every parent, as `--cc` reports them. The old code reached those only through its worktree diff.

`tests/git_process_count_tests.rs` now catches this: the fixture spreads tags, so a `git log` per tag commit makes 6 packages and 30 packages start different numbers of processes. The benchmark also reports time spent in git and, with `CALLISTO_BENCH_SHAPES=1`, the time per command.

Not changed: reading manifests by commit id instead of tag name is about 25% cheaper in git, measured, not the 5x I first estimated, and was not worth reworking the test doubles for. The workspace walk could read manifests in parallel; that is next.

content.text:
No, not for this workload. Of the Rust git libraries, gix is the better one, but neither beats the `git` binary where it matters most for us.

I measured the three operations that dominate Callisto's time on the 4000-package fixture (8002 commits), release builds, same machine:

| operation | system `git` (today) | gix 0.90 | git2 0.21 (libgit2) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| tags with their commits | ~65 ms | ~80 ms | ~90–120 ms |
| manifest at every tag | ~255 ms | ~200 ms | ~1100–1600 ms |
| history with changed paths | ~730 ms | ~3300–3600 ms | ~20,000–22,000 ms |

- **gix vs git2:** gix is far better, about 6× faster on the history walk and 5–8× on blob reads. It's pure Rust, actively developed, and what cargo itself is moving toward. If we use a Rust library, it's gix.
- **gix vs the `git` binary:** `git` wins the history walk by about 4.5×. gix is only ahead on manifest reads, and by about 25%. That's roughly 50 ms at 4000 packages and about 6 ms at 500.
- **Tuning:** I tried an object cache and the repository's own tree diff, and neither changed the history result. gix has no combined-diff support either, so merge commits would still need the binary.
- **Caveats:** These are naive single-threaded spikes, not tuned production code, and another process was compiling on the machine, so expect noise of about ±15%. The history gap is too large for that to change the conclusion.

**My recommendation is to keep system `git` for all of it.** Adopting gix for the manifest reads would add 100+ crates, an ADR reversal and a second code path, for about 6 ms on a realistic workspace. That is not a good trade. I'd revisit if gix's tree diff gets much faster. The spike is in the job's temp directory, not the repo, so nothing needs reverting.

The remaining time is `git log` itself and the sequential directory walk. The walk (~230 ms at 4000 packages) is ours to speed up, so that is what I'll do next: read manifests in parallel during workspace load.

Yes, the gix spike may benefit from a cache supplied by Callisto. The object cache Claude tried stores Git objects. It is different from gix’s diff resource cache. In gix 0.90, Tree::changes().for_each_to_obtain_tree() creates a new diff resource cache on every call; gix also provides for_each_to_obtain_tree_with_cache() to reuse one across calls. Its API documentation (https://github.com/GitoxideLabs/gitoxide/blob/main/gix/src/object/tree/diff/for_each.rs) says reuse avoids repeated setup and I/O.

That matters for an 8,002-commit loop. It is especially worth measuring because Callisto needs changed paths with rename tracking disabled: the diff still sets up the resource cache, while the rename processing that would use it is skipped. If the spike used Repository::diff_tree_to_tree(), that is another poor fit for this workload: it creates the cache per call and collects changes into a Vec, whereas Callisto can consume paths as they arrive.

So I would not call the 4.5× gap gix’s best attainable performance yet. The next fair comparison is the same spike with one reused diff resource cache and streamed changes, checking identical paths and timing the history walk again. Reuse could remove repeated setup; it may not close the whole gap because tree traversal still runs for each commit. Without the spike’s source or that measurement, I can identify the missed optimization opportunity, not quantify its benefit.

Callisto’s current Git access (crates/callisto-model/src/vcs/access.rs:510) uses the system binary, so there is no gix cache to add to production code today.
</pasted_content id="b815">

content.text:
I now have a fair comparison, and it changes the answer: **gix wins at realistic sizes and loses at extreme ones.** On repacked repositories (like real clones), the history walk with changed paths:

| packages / commits | system `git log` | gix low-level | gix |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| 500 / 1000 | 60 ms | **17 ms** | 3.5× faster |
| 2000 / 4000 | 304 ms | **253 ms** | 1.2× faster |
| 4000 / 8000 | ~1020 ms | 3380 ms (2000 ms with a 1 GB pack cache) | 3× slower |

- **The diff resource cache wasn't the lever.** Reusing it moved 4000 packages from 3.3 s to 3.0 s. The sample showed 75% of the time in zlib inflate and memmove, which is delta-chain resolution. The 150 KB `crates` tree is rewritten 8000 times in that fixture. That is the pathological case: one flat directory with 4000 entries and deep history.
- **Manifest reads:** gix is about 25% faster at 4000 packages (~200 ms vs 255 ms). **Tag listing** is a wash (~80 ms vs ~65 ms).
- **Where gix can't do it:** it has no combined-diff for merge commits (`--cc`). A path differs from every parent exactly when it appears in each parent's diff, so I can intersect per-parent diffs. It also has to fall back to the system `git` on any error.

My plan, keeping the binary as the fallback exactly as you asked:
1. Add a native read backend (tags with commits, blob reads, history with changed paths) inside `GitAccess`, with the same results as the CLI path. Writes, signing, trust checks and the worktree diff stay on `git`.
2. Fall back to the CLI on any gix error, an unusual repository (shallow, repository root not the workspace root), or a runtime switch (`CALLISTO_GIT_BACKEND=system`) so I can keep benchmarking both.
3. Test equivalence against the CLI on the same merge and hotfix histories, and keep the process-count gate.
4. Write ADR 13, which supersedes ADR 5, with these numbers and the 4000-entry regression as the revisit trigger. You'd need to accept it, per AGENTS.md.

The one open question is the flat 4000+-entry case, where the CLI is 3× faster. My default is to take gix anyway and set a pack cache of a few hundred MB, because it is rare, and real monorepos spread packages over directories. If you'd rather not regress it, I can read the first tree's size and pick the backend per repository. Starting stage 1 on a new branch off #330.

input.content:
`status` reads the history after every tag to see which packages changed. That cost is linear in commits, and almost all of it is git computing tree diffs. This spreads the diffs over the machine's cores. Stacked on #330.

At 400 packages and 50,000 commits, release build, median of five, 18-core machine:

| command | before ms | after ms |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `status` | 1123 | 328 |
| `version --dry-run` | 124 | 126 |
| `release --dry-run` | 106 | 107 |

Only `status` reads history, so the other two do not move. A 4-core CI runner should see about a 2x gain on `status`, since the diffs scale almost linearly with processes: 906 ms with one `git diff-tree`, 480 with two, 268 with four, 178 with eight for the same 50,000 commits.

How it works:

- `GitAccess::change_history` lists the commits with one `git rev-list --parents --topo-order`, then starts up to eight `git diff-tree --stdin` processes that each take a slice of at least 2000 commits. A merge lists the paths where it differs from every parent (`--cc`), and `--root` includes the first commit's files, as the single `git log` did.
- `-z` prints each commit id and then its paths with no other separator, so the ids asked for are what tell them apart. A path that is not one of the ids asked for before any id is rejected.

Full CI is running on the final change, and I'll ship the PR once it reports `exit=0`. In the meantime, here is where the gix question stands, since you asked me to lean on it hard.

**The cache-sizing hypothesis doesn't hold, and I withdraw my own earlier explanation.** On the instrumented gix pack cache:
- A cold history walk of 8002 commits makes **431,470 cache lookups at a 5% hit rate**, and that rate and the time (3.5–3.9 s) are the same from 8 MB to 2 GB.
- The decoded-object cache doesn't change it either (0 → 2 GB).
- The 2 GB "speedup" I reported earlier was the second of two passes in one process. It is warm-cache reuse; the cold single pass is the same 3.9 s. Two-pass confirmation: 256 MB gives 3.6 s then 3.4 s, 2 GB gives 3.9 s then 1.4 s.

**Why, from the source** (`gix-pack` `resolve_deltas`): it walks a tree's delta chain looking for a cache hit on any element, but afterwards `put`s only the *final* object, never the intermediates. Every tree therefore replays about 15 deltas, copying the whole 150 KB tree each time. Git's delta-base cache stores the bases it passes through, which is why it stays flat as history grows.

**What that means for sizing the cache by repository size:** the working set isn't the problem, since a single pass touches each tree once. It is the chain replay, so a bigger cache can't fix it. What would fix it is caching intermediates in `gix-pack`, which is an upstream change. I can prepare a reproducible wide-tree benchmark and the cache-statistics data above for an upstream issue or patch, as codex suggested. Until that lands, gix is 3–10× slower than `git log` at your scale, so I'm keeping the binary for history and have not added the dependency.

I'll write the ADR only if we adopt gix. Say if you want the upstream issue drafted. Otherwise next is parallelizing the workspace load.

content.text:
You can get most of this, and the biggest win needs no cache at all. I measured the key number first, and I looked at how Entire stores its data.

**What Entire does that's worth copying** (from this repo):
- **Refs are its database.** Each checkpoint is a signed commit at `refs/entire/checkpoints/<2-char shard>/<id>`, with the payload in the commit's tree. It pushes them to `origin` explicitly (`push_checkpoints`) and doesn't fetch them by default.
- **It chains hooks instead of replacing them.** It installs `commit-msg`, `post-commit`, `post-rewrite`, `pre-commit`, `pre-push` and `prepare-commit-msg`, and it keeps your original as `pre-push.pre-entire`.
- **The caution is volume.** It has created **8,613 refs** here, one per checkpoint, which is the kind of ref sprawl we should avoid.

**Ideas, ranked by payoff:**

| idea | cost of `status` at 400 packages / 50k commits | catch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **A. Compare tree ids, not commits.** One `git cat-file --batch-check` asks for each package's directory tree at its tag and at `HEAD`; they match exactly when nothing net-changed. | **22 ms**, flat in commit count (today 328 ms; 1.1 s before this session's work) | Changes meaning: an edit that was later reverted no longer counts as "changed". A test currently pins the old behavior. |
| **B. Per-commit index kept in the git dir.** Commit contents never change, so a cache of "paths changed by commit X" can't go stale. A warm run needs only `rev-list` (75 ms at 50k) plus the new commits. | ~100 ms warm | Exact semantics, but the first run on a fresh clone is cold. |
| **C. Share B through one ref** (the Entire pattern). A single append-only `refs/callisto/index` chain: git's own fetch syncs it incrementally. | cold clones become warm | Treat it as untrusted: verify its signature, use it for `status` only, never for `release` (the committed decision stays the authority). |
| **D. Hooks** (`post-commit`, `post-merge`, `post-rewrite`, `post-checkout`, `reference-transaction`) keep B fresh, chained like Entire's. | helps developer machines and agents committing constantly | fresh CI clones never run hooks, so CI gets nothing; needs `callisto init --hooks` opt-in |
| **E. A `git maintenance` task** (`maintenance.callisto.script`) | the background mode you asked about earlier, with git's own scheduler | same caveat as D |

**My recommendation:** A first, because it removes the history scan entirely. For agentic workflows I think "net change" is arguably the better meaning anyway, since an agent that edits and then reverts shouldn't flag a release. It's your call because it changes a tested behavior. If you want the exact meaning kept, B is next, with C and D/E only once warm-start matters more than the added surface. Do you want A implemented, with the net-change semantics written into the spec and the old test updated?
A not counting as changed should be correct right? It's been reverted so it's no longer changed

Yes, that's the right meaning: if an edit was reverted, the package is back to what was released, so it hasn't changed. That removes the whole history scan (about 22 ms flat, instead of scaling with commits), and it makes parts of #330 and #331 unnecessary. I'm checking where the stack stands before I restructure it.

input.content:
`status` decided which packages changed by reading the history after every tag. That cost grows with the number of commits, which is the wrong thing to scale with in a repository where agents commit all day. A package that was edited and then reverted is back to what was released, so it has not changed. This compares what the package holds now with what it held at its tag, which needs no history at all. Stacked on #328.

At 400 packages and 50,000 commits, release build, median of five:

| command | before ms | after ms |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `status` | 1123 | 116 |
| `version --dry-run` | 124 | 127 |
| `release --dry-run` | 106 | 109 |

`status` is flat in commits: 120 ms at 50,002 commits against 139 ms at 1002 commits (500 packages). It now grows with packages instead, 631 ms at 2000 and 1.4 s at 4000, which is workspace loading and graph work.

What changed:

- A package changed since its last tag when it has no tag, when any directory of it has a different git tree id at `HEAD` than at the tag, or when its tracked files have uncommitted changes. `GitAccess::object_ids` asks `git cat-file --batch-check` for the ids of every package directory at its tag and at `HEAD` in one process: 22 ms for 400 packages. Two ids are equal exactly when the contents are, so nothing is read.
- This changes one behavior: a change that a later commit reverted no longer counts. The `status` spec now says what `changedSinceLastTag` means, and a test that pinned the old meaning is replaced by one for the new.
- A package whose directory did not exist at its tag counts as changed, one that never existed does not, and a tag on an unmerged branch differs from `HEAD` by whatever `HEAD` lacks, as before.
- The tag index tests a template's glob only against the run of tags that begin with its literal prefix, found by binary search in a sorted list, instead of against every tag. At 4000 packages that was about 220 ms of CPU.
- The benchmark fixture now spreads tags over history, as independent releases do, and the benchmark reports the time spent in git and, with `CALLISTO_BENCH_SHAPES=1`, the time per command. `tests/git_process_count_tests.rs` fails when a command starts a different number of git processes for 6 packages than for 30.

An earlier version of this PR read the history in one pass and another read it with parallel `git diff-tree` processes (#331). Both are gone: they were the right fix for the old meaning and are not needed for this one. I also measured gix and git2 for that history read. Neither beat `git log` at 400 packages and 50,000 commits (gix 3 to 10 seconds against 0.93 s), because gix replays delta chains for each tree. With the history read gone there is no operation left where a library pays for its dependencies, so the git binary stays.

content.text:
The remaining cost at many packages falls into three buckets, and the profile says where each one comes from:

| lever | what it fixes | expected gain |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1. Learn manifests from the directory walk, read them in parallel** | The locator stats every directory, then tries to open three canonical manifest files in each one, mostly failing with "not found" (about 24,000 syscalls at 4000 packages). It then reads and parses the existing ones one at a time (~340 ms of reads, ~160 ms of walking). The walker already sees the file names, so only manifests that exist need opening, and reads and parses can run on several threads. | load 728 ms → roughly 200 ms at 4000 packages; about 40 ms → 15 ms at 400 |
| **2. One tag listing instead of two** | The tag index runs `git tag --list`, then a later `git for-each-ref` for the commits. One `for-each-ref` carries both. | one git process; 30–300 ms depending on how many tags are loose refs, which `git gc` packs |
| **3. Cheaper ownership check on tags** | The manifest batch (~280 ms here) exists to confirm that a bare-named tag was made by this package. It could be skipped when no other manifest in the workspace shares the name, which is the common case. | up to ~280 ms at 4000 packages |

The caveat: **at 400 packages `status` is already 116 ms, and these three would take about 30–40 ms off it.** The big wins were the history scans, which are gone. The packages-bound costs are real mainly if you expect the thousands scale.

Where the PRs stand: #330 now carries the tree comparison, rewritten and passing full CI, and #331 is closed as superseded. The stack is #327 → #328 → #330 (stack #332). I'd start with lever 1, since it's the largest and it also helps `version` and `release`, which pay for the same load. Want me to do that next?
What of an extremely large corporate monorepo? That might be thousands of packages

That's the right stress case, and I'd rather measure the curve than extrapolate from 4000. Generating a 10,000-package repository (20,000 commits, repacked) and timing all three commands with peak memory.

content.text:
For thousands of packages the picture is good on history and moderate on package count. Measured on the current code, release build:

| layout | packages | commits | `status` | `version --dry-run` | `release --dry-run` | peak memory |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| nested (100 groups of 100) | 10,000 | 100,000 | 2.85 s | 2.82 s | 3.17 s | 115–180 MB |
| one flat directory | 10,000 | 20,000 | 6.1 s | 4.4 s | 4.1 s | 160–260 MB |

- **History no longer matters.** 100,000 commits cost nothing extra. The flat-directory row is a fixture artifact (one 10,000-entry tree that git scans linearly for each of 20,000 lookups) and no real monorepo is laid out that way.
- **At 10,000 nested packages the time is purely per-package:** about 0.28 ms each, so 400 packages are about 115 ms and 10,000 about 3 s.

Where that 3 s goes (profile of `status`, ~2.2 s sampled):

| cost | share | what it is |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| workspace load | 45% | directory walk (~220 ms), probing three manifest files per directory (~155 ms), opening each manifest a **second time** after the locator already read it (~150 ms), and a quadratic name lookup (below) |
| git | 40% | tag-ownership manifest reads (~315 ms), the tree comparison (~265 ms), the worktree diff (~150 ms) |
| aggregation | 10% | per-package name lookup again |

**One real quadratic in our code:** `IdentityIndex::native_names`, `native_name` and `platforms_of` scan the whole name map for every package, and three call sites do it per package. That is about 12% of the run at 10,000 packages (~0.3 s), growing with the square of the package count.

**What I'd do, with estimated savings at 10,000 packages:**

1. **Reverse index for the name lookups** to remove the quadratic: ~0.3 s, small and safe.
2. **Read each manifest once**: the locator passes its content on instead of `open` re-reading it: ~0.15 s.
3. **Learn which manifests exist from the walk, and read them on several threads**: ~0.4 s.
4. **Skip the tag-ownership read when the name is unambiguous**: ~0.3 s, and it matters most in partial clones, where every skipped read is a skipped network fetch.

Together that takes about 2.85 s to about 1.3 s, a 2× gain. At 400 packages it's 116 ms → about 85 ms.

**One structural idea for very large monorepos:** CI on a huge repository usually checks out shallowly or with a partial clone, and `status` today needs each tag's commit and trees. If the tag annotation also recorded the released package directory's tree id (cache only, never authority; absent means we compare against the tag commit as now), `status` would need just `HEAD`'s trees and the tags, which a shallow checkout with tags can supply. That touches ADR 9, so it's your call whether to take it on.

Want me to start with 1 to 3?
Yes, start with 1 to 3. Should we do 4?

Yes to 1 through 3, starting now. On 4, my recommendation is **not as I described it**, and I'll explain after reading the code once more: that read is a safety check, so skipping it isn't free. First the identity index.

input.content:
With thousands of packages the cost is the packages themselves. A profile of `status` at 10,000 packages found a quadratic in our own code and work that ran one package at a time but did not need to. Stacked on #330.

Release build, median of five, 10,000 packages in 100 groups of 100 and 100,000 commits (`status` and `version` on this machine, 18 cores):

| command | before s | after s |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `status` | 2.85 | 2.27 |
| `version --dry-run` | 2.82 | 2.11 |
| `release --dry-run` | 3.17 | 2.32 |

At 400 packages these commands take 100 to 120 ms and move by under 10%. This work is for the large end.

What changed:

- `IdentityIndex::native_name`, `native_names` and `platforms_of` scanned the whole name map for each package, and three callers did that once per package, so the cost grew with the square of the package count (about 12% of the run at 10,000). The index now keeps a by-package view, built on first use and rebuilt when either map changes size, so each lookup is direct. Lookups return what they did before, in the same order, and a clone starts without the view.
- The locator reads and parses every directory's manifests on up to eight threads. Everything that decides, reports or fails still runs in walk order, so errors and warnings are the same ones in the same order. `parallel::map_in_parallel` keeps results in input order and runs a short list on the calling thread.
- The manifests that `resolve_packages` opens one at a time are first opened on several threads into the same cache. One that fails to open is opened again one at a time, which reports it as before.
- `check_partial_run` read and parsed each package's own `Cargo.toml` twice to find the paths that can set its version. It now does it once per manifest.

Not changed, and why:

- Each package directory is looked up in git trees at its tag and at `HEAD`. In a flat directory of thousands of packages that is quadratic inside git (a 6.1 s `status` at 10,000 packages in one directory against 2.27 s nested), but no real monorepo is laid out that way, so I measured the nested layout.
- The check that a bare-named tag was made by this package reads each package's manifest at its tag (about 300 ms at 10,000). Skipping it when the name is unique among current packages would drop the protection against a tag made by a package that has since been renamed or removed, so it stays.
- Reading each manifest only once would mean carrying its text through `ProjectRoot`, a public type. Opening them ahead on several threads takes most of that cost without changing the API.

# 9. A tag's identity is its commit and being annotated

Status: Accepted (implemented in #154)

## Context

- A rerun adopts effects that already landed (ADR 3), so it must decide whether an existing tag is the one it planned.
- The local check read the tag with `git for-each-ref` and compared the target commit and the annotation text. The remote check uses `git ls-remote`, which returns the tag object and peeled commit but not the annotation text, so it compared only the commit.
- The same repository state could therefore be adopted or rejected depending on whether the remote tag had been fetched.

## Decision

An existing tag is the planned tag when it names the planned commit and is annotated. Annotation text is not compared, locally or remotely. A lightweight tag or a tag on another commit is a conflict (E167) and is never adopted.

## Options considered

- **Compare the annotation text on both sides** — rejected: the remote side needs the tag object fetched first, and a tag created by a person or an earlier template would block every rerun.
- **Keep the split (text locally, commit remotely)** — rejected: the outcome depends on fetch state.

## Consequences

- Local and remote checks agree.
- A tag with a different message is adopted. The receipt records only the peeled commit (`ProviderEvidenceV1::GitTag { peeled_commit }` in `crates/callisto-model/src/release_observation.rs`), and `gh release create --verify-tag` checks only that the tag exists.

## Enforcement

- Tests in `crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release/provider/tag.rs` for local and remote observation (different annotation text is adopted; lightweight and other-commit tags conflict).
- REL-RERUN-02 and REL-RERUN-03 in `docs/specs/release.json`.

## Revisit when

- Something downstream starts reading the annotation text (release notes, signing policy, provenance).

## Sources

- Owner decision, `docs/projects/ROAD-TO-V1.md` "v1 fix plan" decisions (2026-09-25)
- The fix in this PR: "fix: stop comparing tag annotation text in release rerun observation"

# Architecture decision records

- [1. Changesets-compatible change records](0001-changesets-compatible-change-records.md) — `.changeset/*.md` in `@changesets/cli`'s format, commit inference opt-in; guardrail: do not make Conventional Commits the primary input or change the file format without a new ADR.
- [2. The committed version decision is the release authority](0002-committed-decision-is-release-authority.md) — CI verifies the merged commit against the decision `callisto version --emit-decision` committed; guardrail: do not re-derive cascade or group policy after merge without a new ADR.
- [3. Reruns observe and adopt landed effects; no persisted execution state](0003-reruns-adopt-landed-effects.md) — every run observes providers and adopts what landed, state stays in memory; guardrail: do not add a persisted execution state file or recovery commands without a new ADR.
- [4. Ecosystem tools publish and own authentication](0004-ecosystem-tools-publish-and-own-auth.md) — `cargo`, the npm-family tools, `twine` and `gh` publish with their own credentials; guardrail: do not add native registry clients or a credential pre-flight without a new ADR.
- [5. System git only](0005-system-git-only.md) — every Git command in the `callisto` binary runs the system `git`; guardrail: do not add gix or a second Git backend without a new ADR.
- [6. moon integrates through a proto plugin, not a WASM extension](0006-moon-through-proto-plugin-not-wasm-extension.md) — moon users install the native CLI with a proto TOML plugin; guardrail: do not add a moon WASM extension or WASM build without a new ADR.
- [7. Platform packages are owned through optionalDependencies and release with their owner](0007-platform-packages-owned-through-optional-dependencies.md) — an `os`+`cpu` package with one owner releases with that owner; guardrail: do not require fixed-group entries or explicit config for platform packages without a new ADR.
- [8. Format-preserving manifest writes gated by ApplyPermit](0008-format-preserving-writes-gated-by-apply-permit.md) — `toml_edit` and fingerprinted JSON through `atomic_write(&ApplyPermit)`; guardrail: do not use typed serde round-trips for TOML, unfingerprinted `package.json` rewrites, regex edits or unpermitted writes without a new ADR.

# 13. A tag's annotation can carry hints that skip work, never identity

Status: Proposed

## Context

- ADR 9 makes a tag's identity its commit and being annotated, and does not compare annotation text: the remote check (`git ls-remote`) cannot read it, and a hand-made or older tag would otherwise block every rerun. It names its revisit trigger: something downstream starts reading the annotation text.
- Two reads dominate a workspace of thousands of packages. Confirming that a bare-named tag was made by this package reads its manifest at the tag (about 300 ms at 10,000 packages). Deciding whether a package changed since its tag compares each of its directories' tree ids at the tag with `HEAD` (about 265 ms), which needs the tag's commit trees.
- Callisto knows both facts when it creates the tag: who the package is and what each of its directories held in the release commit.
- A shallow or partial checkout has to fetch those commits and trees, or cannot answer.

## Decision

- The annotation Callisto writes keeps `Release {tag}` as its first line and adds git trailers: `Callisto-Hints: 1`, `Callisto-Package: <canonical ref>` and one `Callisto-Tree: <directory> <tree id>` per package directory (`.` for a root package). The trailers are read by the same `git for-each-ref` that lists the tags.
- A hint only lets a read be skipped. It never makes a tag adopted and never decides identity; ADR 9 is unchanged. Release effects are still derived from commits and the committed decision (ADR 2).
- Every consumer works without a hint. A hint is used only when the tag is annotated, `Callisto-Hints` is a version this release understands, the trailer it needs parses, and, for the owner, it names this package's canonical ref or, for the trees, it has an entry for every directory of the package. In every other case, including a hint that names another package, the consumer does the read it does today and that read decides.
- Existing tags are never rewritten. The fallback is permanent, not a migration step.

## Options considered

- **A ref namespace holding an index** (`refs/callisto/...`): rejected. It is extra refs to fetch and push, it can go stale against the tags, and it needs its own trust story. The tag is already the per-release record and travels with it.
- **A persistent local cache keyed by commit**: rejected for this purpose. It helps warm local runs only, and CI starts cold.
- **Skip the owner check when the name is unique among current packages**: rejected. It loses the protection against a tag made by a package that has since been renamed or removed, which is the case the check exists for.
- **Compare annotation text for identity**: rejected for the reasons in ADR 9.
- **A git note**: rejected. Notes are not fetched by default and are not part of the tag object.

## Consequences

- At 10,000 packages the two reads are about 0.55 s of a 2.2 s command; at 400 packages they are tens of milliseconds. The larger value is a shallow or partial checkout that no longer has to read the tag commit's trees or manifest.
- The annotation text of new tags changes, so a sealed intent that carries it has a different digest than the same release would have had. Existing intents are unaffected.
- A tag object is immutable, so a hint cannot go stale. It can be wrong if someone writes a false annotation, which is the trust ADR 9 already extends to any annotated tag on the planned commit; a wrong hint changes what a read reports, never what an effect does.
- Hints and the fallback are two code paths per consumer, each tested against the same repository.

## Enforcement

- For each consumer, tests for no hint at all (a lightweight tag, an annotation that is only `Release {tag}`, an unknown hint version, a missing, garbled or partial trailer, a hint naming another package, a directory with no entry) that assert the same result as today.
- An equivalence test that builds one repository with and without hints and asserts the same `status` and tag index.
- Spec criteria in `docs/specs/release.json` and `docs/specs/cli.json` stating that a hint never changes a result.

## Revisit when

- A consumer needs a hint to be authoritative.
- Tags become signed or carry provenance that reads the annotation differently.
- A measured saving at the sizes in use is too small to justify the second path.

## Sources

- ADR 9, its revisit trigger.
- PR #330 and PR #333: the profiles and timings at 400 to 10,000 packages.

# michi 0.6.0: what Callisto was waiting on is published

From the michi session, 2026-10-23. `michi-core`, `michi-graph` and `michi-pipeline` 0.6.0 are on crates.io (one version for every michi package now). NEXT-WORK.md's "Waiting on michi: … pipeline precheck, poll step, group deadline, per-key concurrency" is done. Full semantics: michi's `docs/spec/08-pipeline-execution.md` and `docs/spec/09-graph.md`.

## michi-pipeline 0.6.0, mapped to the brief

| Brief item | API | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2. Precheck | `Replay::Prechecked` + `Step::precheck(ctx) -> Precheck::{Applied, NotApplied, Unknown}` | Runs before every attempt, after breaker admission; not counted by the breaker or retry budget. `Applied` ends the step `CompletedEarlier` without running it (fresh run or resume). `Unknown` runs nothing: `NotRun(Unverified)`, or the prior attempt's `OutcomeUnknown`. Return `NotApplied` only with proof of absence (a stale npm packument is not proof). |
| 3. Poll step | `poll_step(PollSchedule::default(), check)` with `Readiness::{Ready, NotYet(observed)}` | Default schedule: now, then 2s/4s/8s/16s, then every 30s. One attempt from the executor's view: never draws from the retry budget. A poll step is bounded by its deadline (`AttemptBound::Deadline`), not the attempt timeout, so give it a `deadline` or a `deadline_group`; the attempt timeout then bounds each check. When the window ends it fails with `DeadlinePassed` naming the last observation (not applied; resume polls again). |
| 4. Shared deadline | `ExecStep::deadline_group(key)` + `ExecOptions::group_deadline(key, Duration)` | The window opens at the group's first dispatch, so verify steps started at different times expire together. A member that would start after the window closes is never invoked and ends `Failed` with `DeadlinePassed`. |
| 5. Per-key concurrency | `ExecStep::concurrency_key(key)` + `ExecOptions::concurrency_limit(key, n)` | "At most N in flight per registry". A full key waits in the dispatch loop without blocking other keys; earliest-declared runnable step goes first. |
| 6. Blocking-step adapter | `step_blocking(\|ctx\| …)` (`.idempotent()` too) | Runs on `spawn_blocking`. The closure gets a cancellation token that fires on run cancel or when the executor stops waiting (timeout, grace, drop): use it to kill a child `cargo`/`npm` process. A non-idempotent step never runs two closures at once while an abandoned one is still running (within one process). |
| (not asked) Effects | `ExecutionError::{failed, refused, rejected, transient}`, `Effect::{NotApplied, Unknown}` | Every failure says whether its effect may have landed. A non-idempotent step whose effect is unknown ends `OutcomeUnknown` and resume holds it until verified or prechecked: matches "never retry an effect blindly". |
| (not asked) Durable starts | `ExecOptions::durable_starts(observer)` with a `DurableObserver` | A step runs only after `record_start` saved its in-flight marker; matches "`Attempting` only after a proof". |
| 7. Typed outputs | not built | Waiting for the trial to show a need. |

## michi-graph: per-edge readiness for the publish wave (in review, michi PR #48)

NPM-PUBLISH-WAVE.md phase 2 needs readiness that differs by edge: a sibling registry publish may follow once its prerequisite publish is *issued*, while tags and forge releases wait for it to be *confirmed*. PR #48 makes `Dag<K, E>` keep edge kinds and adds:

- `dag.prerequisite_edges(ix) -> &[(NodeIx, E)]`
- `dag.ready_by_edge(|key| eligible, |prerequisite, kind| satisfied)`: every kept edge is judged with its kind.

Model the release as nodes with edge kinds (for example `Needs::Issued` for registry-to-registry edges, `Needs::Confirmed` for everything else) and let `ready_by_edge` replace an `issued`-aware `eligible_operations`. It ships in the next michi release.

The decision, in short:

- The annotation keeps `Release {tag}` as its first line and adds trailers: `Callisto-Hints: 1`, `Callisto-Package: <canonical ref>` and one `Callisto-Tree: <directory> <tree id>` per package directory. They are read by the `git for-each-ref` that already lists the tags.
- A hint only lets a read be skipped. It never makes a tag adopted and never decides identity, so ADR 9 is unchanged and release effects are still derived from commits and the committed decision.
- Every consumer works with no hint at all, for any reason: a lightweight or hand-made tag, a tag from before this change, an unknown hint version, a missing or garbled trailer, a hint naming another package, a directory with no entry. In each case it does today's read and gets today's answer. Existing tags are never rewritten.

Rejected: a `refs/callisto/...` index, a persistent local cache, skipping the owner check when the name is unique among current packages (it loses the protection against a tag made by a package since renamed or removed), comparing annotation text for identity, and a git note.

Honest cost and benefit: about 0.55 s of 2.2 s at 10,000 packages, but only tens of milliseconds at 400. The larger value is shallow or partial checkouts that no longer need the tag commit's trees. The annotation text of new tags changes, so a sealed intent that carries it has a different digest than the same release had before.

ADR 9's revisit trigger is "something downstream starts reading the annotation text", which this does, so I added the new record instead of editing ADR 9.
